title: DfE Decoded #160: Phonics Is Back to 2019 Levels — But That Isn’t the Most Interesting Bit
author: Paul Urry
summary: Paul Urry reads the 2026 English phonics screening check results for school leaders and argues the headline is the least interesting part. The 82 percent national pass rate matches 2018 and 2019, but the pass mark was 31 instead of the usual 32, which is a reminder that the check is a screening measure and not a full judgement of reading. Year 2 attainment has stayed at 89 percent for three years, leaving about one child in nine below the standard. The disadvantage gap is still 17 points, the SEN figure of 46 percent is the highest recorded, and the first-language English and EAL groups now match at 82 percent. Large differences remain by ethnicity, by month of birth (87 percent for September-born against 76 percent for August-born) and by sex. Urry advises leaders to look under their own headline percentage at which children are still struggling and why, and to use the national data as a prompt and not as a league table.
points: The expected-standard threshold moved from 32 to 31 for the first time since 2012, so raw comparisons over time need a caution.
Year 2 attainment has been flat at 89 percent for three years, which makes the children still below standard a more useful school-level group than the Year 1 headline.
The 17-point disadvantage gap survived a rise for both groups, showing that a better national average does not mean greater equity.
The EAL gap has disappeared and SEN attainment hit a record 46 percent, undermining lazy assumptions about what those labels predict.
Summer-born pupils trail September-born pupils by around 11 to 12 points, so identical scores can reflect different developmental distances.
quotes: For the first time since the phonics screening check was introduced in 2012, the mark needed to meet the expected standard changed.
And perhaps more importantly, it reminds us why a phonics screening score is a screening measure rather than a complete judgement about a child’s reading.
It means that roughly one in nine children is still not reaching the phonics standard by the end of Year 2.
A rising national average does not necessarily mean greater equity. You can improve overall outcomes while leaving the gap almost untouched.
Speaking another language first is not, in itself, an indicator of lower academic potential.
An August-born child scoring 30 and a September-born child scoring 30 have achieved the same score. They have not necessarily travelled the same developmental distance to get there.
Because 82% tells us something about the system. It tells us rather less about an individual six-year-old.
Not as a league table. As a prompt to look more closely at the children behind our own numbers.
